pos: n. (proper name; a son of David born in Jerusalem)
etymology: Hebrew Yibchar, he chooses or chosen, from bachar, to choose.
biblical_def: Ibhar is a son of David born in Jerusalem. After David came from Hebron, “David took him more concubines and wives out of Jerusalem, after he was come from Hebron: and there were yet sons and daughters born to David” (2 Samuel 5:13). The list follows Solomon: “Ibhar also, and Elishua, and Nepheg, and Japhia” (2 Samuel 5:15). Chronicles gives him twice (1 Chronicles 3:6; 14:5), and sums the household: “These were all the sons of David, beside the sons of the concubines, and Tamar their sister” (1 Chronicles 3:9). Nothing is recorded of Ibhar's life. His name means he chooses, and it stands beside Solomon's, the son whom God chose to build His house. Of all David's many sons, God chose one for the throne and the promise. Scripture also records honestly that David multiplied wives, against the law of the king in Deuteronomy 17:17, and the sorrows of his house grew from that disobedience.

pos: n. (proper name; sixth son of David, born in Hebron)
etymology: Hebrew Yithre'am, abundance of the people or remnant of the people, from yether, remainder, abundance, and 'am, people.
biblical_def: Ithream is the sixth son born to David in Hebron. “And unto David were sons born in Hebron: and his firstborn was Amnon, of Ahinoam the Jezreelitess” (2 Samuel 3:2). The list ends: “And the sixth, Ithream, by Eglah David's wife. These were born to David in Hebron” (2 Samuel 3:5). Chronicles repeats it: “the sixth, Ithream by Eglah his wife” (1 Chronicles 3:3), and adds, “These six were born unto him in Hebron; and there he reigned seven years and six months” (1 Chronicles 3:4). The Hebron sons include Amnon, who defiled his sister, Absalom, who rebelled, and Adonijah, who seized the throne. Ithream is not named in any of those sorrows; his name alone survives. His mother Eglah is the only one of the six mothers called David's wife in so many words. The Hebron list shows how a king's house may hold both quiet sons and violent ones, and how the promise passed over all of them to Solomon, born later in Jerusalem.

pos: n. (proper name; the spy of Issachar, and one of David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Yig'al, he redeems or he will redeem, from ga'al, to redeem.
biblical_def: Igal is the name of two men in the Old Testament. The first was the spy of Issachar sent to search Canaan: “Of the tribe of Issachar, Igal the son of Joseph” (Numbers 13:7). The LORD had commanded, “of every tribe of their fathers shall ye send a man, every one a ruler among them” (Numbers 13:2). Igal was one of the ten who returned with the evil report: “We be not able to go up against the people; for they are stronger than we” (Numbers 13:31). Those men “died by the plague before the LORD” (Numbers 14:37). The second Igal is among David's mighty men: “Igal the son of Nathan of Zobah, Bani the Gadite” (2 Samuel 23:36). The two men bear the same name, he redeems, and stand at opposite ends of Israel's story: one who doubted the promise of the land, and one who fought to establish the kingdom in it. The parallel list in Chronicles reads differently at this place (1 Chronicles 11:38).

pos: n. (proper name; an Ammonite among David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Tseleq, cleft, fissure, from a root meaning to split.
biblical_def: Zelek the Ammonite is one of David's mighty men. “Zelek the Ammonite, Naharai the Beerothite, armourbearer to Joab the son of Zeruiah” (2 Samuel 23:37). Chronicles repeats him (1 Chronicles 11:39). The law said, “An Ammonite or Moabite shall not enter into the congregation of the LORD; even to their tenth generation” (Deuteronomy 23:3), yet an Ammonite stood among the chief of David's warriors, those “who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom” (1 Chronicles 11:10). The roster of the thirty includes foreigners: Uriah the Hittite, Ithmah the Moabite, Zelek the Ammonite. They had left their own peoples to serve Israel's king. Zelek is a quiet foreshadowing of the gospel, in which strangers from every nation are gathered to the Son of David, and the dividing wall is broken down. The Ammonites as a nation remained enemies of Israel; an Ammonite who joined himself to David was counted among his mighty men.

David had Moabite blood through his great-grandmother Ruth, who said to Naomi, “thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God” (Ruth 1:16). When Saul hunted him, David sent his parents to the king of Moab for safety: “Let my father and my mother, I pray thee, come forth, and be with you, till I know what God will do for me” (1 Samuel 22:3). Ithmah is one of the men who “strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom” (1 Chronicles 11:10). Like Ruth before him, a Moabite came under the wings of the God of Israel by joining His anointed. pos: n. (proper name; a son of Elnaam among David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Yeribay, he contends or the LORD contends, from rib, to strive, to plead a cause.
biblical_def: Jeribai is one of David's mighty men, named with his brother. “Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite” (1 Chronicles 11:46). He belongs to the Chronicler's added names, men “who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom, and with all Israel, to make him king, according to the word of the LORD concerning Israel” (1 Chronicles 11:10). His name means he contends, the word used of God pleading the cause of His people. Two sons of one father served David together. Their strength was not their own: “It is God that girdeth me with strength, and maketh my way perfect” (Psalm 18:32), David sang, and the men who fought beside him shared the same confession. Elnaam's sons were his heritage: “Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward” (Psalm 127:3). A father who gave two sons to the service of the LORD's anointed had a quiver full.

pos: n. (proper name; a son of Elnaam among David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Yoshawyah, the LORD makes to dwell or the LORD is equality; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Joshaviah is the brother of Jeribai, and both sons of Elnaam served among David's mighty men. “Eliel the Mahavite, and Jeribai, and Joshaviah, the sons of Elnaam, and Ithmah the Moabite” (1 Chronicles 11:46). The Chronicler expands the roster of Samuel with the names of men who came to David as the kingdom grew: “For at that time day by day there came to David to help him, until it was a great host, like the host of God” (1 Chronicles 12:22). Brothers who fought side by side reflect the song of David: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!” (Psalm 133:1). Nothing more is recorded of Joshaviah. His place on the roster is a reminder that the kingdom of David, like the kingdom of Christ, was built by many whose names few remember, but whom God records. “The glory of young men is their strength” (Proverbs 20:29), and these brothers spent theirs in the service of the LORD's anointed.

pos: n. (proper name; the Mesobaite among David's mighty men)
etymology: Hebrew Ya'asi'el, made by God, from 'asah, to make, and 'el, God.
biblical_def: Jasiel the Mesobaite is the last name in the Chronicler's roster of David's mighty men. “Eliel, and Obed, and Jasiel the Mesobaite” (1 Chronicles 11:47). The list began, “These also are the chief of the mighty men whom David had, who strengthened themselves with him in his kingdom” (1 Chronicles 11:10), and ends with him. The meaning of Mesobaite is uncertain; some connect it with Zobah, the Aramean kingdom David conquered: “David smote also Hadadezer, the son of Rehob, king of Zobah” (2 Samuel 8:3). If so, Jasiel was another foreigner joined to David, like Igal of Zobah in Samuel's list. A man of the same name, Jaasiel son of Abner, was later ruler of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 27:21), in the Hebrew spelled alike. Jasiel's name confesses that God made him; his service shows what God made him for.

pos: n. (proper name; a Benjamite archer who joined David at Ziklag)
etymology: Hebrew Yezi'el, assembly of God or God sprinkles; the sense is uncertain.
biblical_def: Jeziel is one of the Benjamites who left Saul to join David at Ziklag. “Now these are they that came to David to Ziklag, while he yet kept himself close because of Saul the son of Kish: and they were among the mighty men, helpers of the war” (1 Chronicles 12:1). “They were armed with bows, and could use both the right hand and the left in hurling stones and shooting arrows out of a bow, even of Saul's brethren of Benjamin” (1 Chronicles 12:2). The list names “Jeziel, and Pelet, the sons of Azmaveth” (1 Chronicles 12:3). These were Saul's own kinsmen. They came while David was still a fugitive, when joining him meant danger, not reward. They chose the man God had anointed over the man of their own tribe who held the throne. “For at that time day by day there came to David to help him, until it was a great host” (1 Chronicles 12:22). Jeziel and his brother are pictures of those who come to Christ in His humiliation, before His kingdom is seen.

pos: n. (proper name; a Gibeonite captain over David's thirty)
etymology: Hebrew Yishma'yahu, the LORD hears, from shama', to hear, and Yah.
biblical_def: Ismaiah the Gibeonite is one of the men who came to David at Ziklag, honored as a leader of the thirty. “And Ismaiah the Gibeonite, a mighty man among the thirty, and over the thirty; and Jeremiah, and Jahaziel, and Johanan, and Josabad the Gederathite” (1 Chronicles 12:4). The Gibeonites were not Israelites. They had deceived Joshua into a covenant, and “Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD” (Joshua 9:27). Saul later broke that covenant: “Saul sought to slay them in his zeal to the children of Israel and Judah” (2 Samuel 21:2). A Gibeonite had every reason to fear Saul, and Ismaiah came to David instead. He rose from a servant people to be over the thirty. His name means the LORD hears; God heard the cry of the Gibeonites against Saul's bloodguilt, and in David's service a son of that people was exalted.
